questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.topic: Radians as a unit of angle
questions.learningObjective: define one radian as the angle whose arc equals the radius
questions.stem: Which statement defines the angle that measures exactly one radian?

options.text: the central angle whose intercepted arc equals the radius in length
the central angle whose intercepted arc equals half the circumference
options.misconception: confuses one radian with a half turn, which is actually pi radians

options.text: the angle formed when one full turn is divided into 360 equal parts
options.misconception: describes a degree, the smaller unit built from 360 equal parts

options.text: the angle inside a sector whose area equals the area of the circle
options.misconception: matches arc sectors to areas instead of arc length to the radius

questions.explanation: A radian is defined by an arc that is exactly as long as the radius, so the angle and the arc it cuts off carry the same numerical size when the arc is measured in radius units. The half-turn distractor mixes up radian and straight angle measures, since a half turn is pi radians, not one. The 360-part distractor is the definition of a degree, and the area distractor replaces the length comparison that defines the radian with an area comparison that never even fixes the angle.
questions.hint: Compare the length of the cut-off arc with the radius of the same circle.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: conclude that a full turn measures 2*pi radians from circumference
questions.stem: A wheel of radius 10 centimetres rolls one complete revolution, and the track it lays down is 20*pi centimetres long. How many radians is one full revolution?

options.text: 2*pi radians, since the arc laid down is 2*pi radii in length
pi radians, since the arc laid down is pi radii in length
options.misconception: halves the circumference, treating a full turn as a half turn

options.text: 20*pi radians, since the arc is 20*pi centimetres long
options.misconception: keeps the centimetre count instead of restating it in radius units

options.text: 360 radians, since one revolution is the measure of a full turn
options.misconception: substitutes the degree count for the radian count of the same turn

questions.explanation: A full revolution lays down the circumference, 2*pi*r centimetres, and dividing that arc by the radius leaves 2*pi, so a full turn is 2*pi radians. The pi option is the half-turn, which lays down only pi radii. The 20*pi option forgets that the radian count is a ratio, so the centimetres must be divided by 10. The 360 option swaps in the degree count, which is a different numbering of the same turn.
questions.hint: Divide the arc length the wheel lays down by the wheel radius.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: explain why the sector area formula contains a factor of one half
questions.stem: Explain why the area of a sector of radius r and central angle theta radians is one half r squared times theta.

answer.exemplar: The sector is a fraction of the whole disc, and that fraction is theta over 2*pi, because 2*pi radians is the full turn. Multiplying the circle area pi*r squared by theta over 2*pi cancels the pi and leaves r squared times theta over 2. The one half survives because the cancellation removes a factor of 2 from the denominator, which is exactly the 2 in 2*pi radians per turn. Equivalently, the sector can be split into many thin triangles, each with two sides of length r and included angle theta, and the area of a triangle is one half times base times height, which again produces the factor of one half before the sum is taken.

questions.explanation: A strong answer connects the sector to a share of the circle and shows where the surviving one half comes from in the cancellation, or reproduces it by summing thin triangles.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: explain why cosine is the x-coordinate on the unit circle
questions.stem: Explain why the cosine of an angle in standard position equals the x-coordinate of its terminal point on the unit circle.

answer.exemplar: An angle in standard position has its vertex at the origin, its initial side on the positive x-axis and its terminal side crossing the unit circle at some point. Dropping a perpendicular from that point to the x-axis forms a right triangle whose hypotenuse is the radius of the circle, which has length one, and the leg that lies along the x-axis is exactly the x-coordinate of the terminal point. Cosine is defined as the adjacent leg over the hypotenuse, so it equals that x-coordinate divided by one, which is simply the x-coordinate. The radius being one is what removes the division, and the sine of the angle is handled by the same triangle, giving the y-coordinate instead.

questions.explanation: A strong response constructs the right triangle, identifies the x-coordinate as the adjacent leg, and notes that the radius of one makes the hypotenuse vanish from the ratio.
questions.hint: Drop a perpendicular from the terminal point to the x-axis and read the adjacent leg over the hypotenuse.

On the unit circle the reference angle fixes the size of the y-coordinate, which is the sine, while the quadrant fixes only its sign. questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: explain why the radian measure of an angle is independent of the radius
questions.stem: Explain why the radian measure of a fixed angle is the same no matter how large the circle is.

answer.exemplar: A radian is defined by an intercepted arc that is exactly as long as the radius, so the radian measure of an angle is the ratio of the arc length to the radius. If the circle is scaled by any factor, both the arc and the radius scale by that same factor, so the factor cancels in the ratio and the measure is unchanged. This is what makes radians a unit of angle rather than a unit of length, and it is why a conversion table lists the same radian value for an angle on a coin and on a running track.

questions.explanation: A strong answer states that the radian measure is a ratio of two lengths and shows that a scaling of the circle multiplies both quantities equally.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: explain why one radian is about 57.3 degrees rather than a reciprocal factor
questions.stem: Explain why one radian is about 57.3 degrees while one degree is only about 0.0175 radians, using the half-turn anchor.

answer.exemplar: Both conversions come from the same fact, that pi radians and 180 degrees measure the same half turn, so a change of scale is a single fixed ratio in each direction and the two factors are reciprocals. Dividing the radian count by the degree count for that shared angle gives pi over 180, which is about 0.01745, so one degree is that fraction of a radian. Inverting the ratio gives 180 over pi, about 57.2958, so one radian spans that many degrees. The asymmetry in size is simply the fact that a half turn is divided into 180 degree parts but into only about 3.14 radian parts, so each degree part must be much smaller than each radian part.

questions.explanation: A strong response derives both factors from the shared half turn and shows that their difference in size follows from 180 parts compared with about 3.14 parts.
questions.hint: Start from pi radians equals 180 degrees and divide one way, then the other.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: identify two adjacent quadrant points correctly
questions.stem: Which two points below are terminal points on the unit circle in the second quadrant? Select two.

options.text: the point (-sqrt(3)/2, 1/2), which lies halfway up the left side at 5*pi over 6 radians
the point (-1/2, sqrt(3)/2), which lies higher up the left side at 2*pi over 3 radians
the point (sqrt(3)/2, 1/2), which has a negative cosine and a positive sine
options.misconception: describes a first quadrant point while claiming the second quadrant sign pattern

options.text: the point (-sqrt(3)/2, -1/2), which has a negative x-coordinate and a negative sine
options.misconception: places the point below the x-axis, where quadrant three and not quadrant two lives

questions.explanation: In quadrant two the x-coordinate is negative while the y-coordinate stays positive, and both (-sqrt(3)/2, 1/2) at 5*pi over 6 and (-1/2, sqrt(3)/2) at 2*pi over 3 satisfy that. Option C has both coordinates positive, so it is a first quadrant point, and option D has a negative y-coordinate, so it is a third quadrant point.
questions.hint: Require a negative x-coordinate together with a positive y-coordinate.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: recall the terminal point of a quadrant three special angle
questions.stem: Which point is the terminal point on the unit circle for an angle of 4*pi/3 radians?

options.text: the point (-1/2, -sqrt(3)/2), since the reference angle pi over 3 supplies the sizes and quadrant three flips both signs
the point (-sqrt(3)/2, -1/2), since the reference angle pi over 6 supplies the sizes and quadrant three flips both signs
options.misconception: uses a pi over 6 reference angle, which belongs to 7*pi over 6 rather than to this angle

options.text: the point (-1/2, sqrt(3)/2), since only the x-coordinate changes sign in the third quadrant
options.misconception: flips only the x-coordinate, which is what quadrant two and not quadrant three does

options.text: the point (1/2, -sqrt(3)/2), since the angle is more than pi and only the y-coordinate is negative
options.misconception: keeps the x-coordinate positive, which is a fourth quadrant pattern

questions.explanation: The reference angle of 4*pi over 3 is pi over 3, which fixes the sizes as one half and root 3 over 2, and quadrant three makes both coordinates negative, giving (-1/2, -sqrt(3)/2). Option B names the wrong reference angle, and options C and D get the sign pattern wrong.
questions.hint: Take one third of pi from the nearest axis for the reference angle, then apply the quadrant three signs.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: explain why the special angles come in complementary pairs on the unit circle
questions.stem: Explain why the terminal points for pi over 6 and pi over 3 radians have their coordinates swapped.

answer.exemplar: The two angles add to pi over 2, which is a right angle, so they are complementary. On the unit circle the terminal points of complementary angles are mirror images across the diagonal line y equals x, and a reflection across that diagonal exchanges the two coordinates. That is why the point for pi over 6, which is (root 3 over 2, one half), becomes the point for pi over 3, which is (one half, root 3 over 2). The same statement is usually read off the identity that the cosine of an angle equals the sine of its complement, because the x-coordinate of one terminal point is the y-coordinate of the mirrored one.

questions.explanation: A strong response identifies the complementary relationship, the mirror across the diagonal, and the resulting coordinate swap, and links it to the cosine and sine identity.
questions.hint: Add the two angles and reflect one terminal point across the diagonal y equals x.
